title: IUL Policy Review: In-Force Illustration | Honorbrook
description: Own an IUL? Ask the insurer for an in-force illustration, read the guaranteed column first, then check loans, premium and surrender charges before any change.
lead: To check an indexed universal life policy you already own, ask the insurer for an in-force illustration and read the guaranteed column first. It shows how long the policy stays in force at your current premium if only the guaranteed credits and charges apply. This page covers how to ask for one, what to check, and what a review can lead to.
article_html:
What an in-force illustration is

An in-force illustration is the insurer’s updated projection of your own policy. It starts from today’s cash value, loan balance and premium, and shows the years ahead. The NAIC model rule on life insurance illustrations defines it as an illustration furnished after a policy has been in force for one year or more.

Your annual statement looks back at the past year. The illustration looks forward.

How to ask the insurer for one

  1. Find your policy number and the insurer’s service contact on your annual statement.
  2. Call or write as the policy owner. Ask for “an in-force illustration at my current premium.”
  3. Ask that it show guaranteed and non-guaranteed values year by year, with any loan included.

Under the model rule, the insurer furnishes one when the owner asks. Its notice to owners says you may ask once a year without charge. If nothing arrives within 30 days, it says to contact your state insurance department. States decide whether and how to adopt the model, so your state’s rule can differ.

Guaranteed and non-guaranteed columns

ColumnWhat it assumesHow to use it
GuaranteedOnly the values, credits and charges the policy guarantees.Read it first. Find the year it reaches zero.
Non-guaranteed (current)The current non-guaranteed credits and charges continue unchanged every year.Treat it as one possible path, not a promise.

The model rule puts guaranteed values first and shows a zero in any year with no guaranteed value. Non-guaranteed values must carry a statement that the insurer can change the assumptions and that actual results may be more or less favorable.

Four points for every IUL owner: The current cap and participation rate are non-guaranteed. The insurer can change them within the limits in your policy. Policy charges come out of the cash value. Surrender charges reduce what you receive if you cancel during the surrender period. The guaranteed column is only as strong as the insurer’s ability to pay claims.

Five questions to check

  1. Does the guaranteed column end, and when? Find the first year it shows zero. If that is earlier than you need coverage, ask what premium carries the policy to the age you choose.
  2. Is a loan balance growing? Compare the loan line on this year’s statement with last year’s. See how policy loans work.
  3. Is your premium below what was illustrated? Compare what you paid with your original illustration. The NAIC Life Insurance Buyer’s Guide says universal life lets you choose a flexible premium pattern as long as you pay enough to keep the policy in force.
  4. When do surrender charges end? Ask for the charge by policy year before any withdrawal, reduction or cancellation.
  5. What are the current cap and participation rate? Ask for today’s rates on each index account you use, and the minimums the policy allows.

A policy that needs attention does not mean anyone did something wrong.

What a review can lead to

We look first at ways to keep the policy you have.

  • Keep it and adjust the premium to a figure the insurer illustrates.
  • Lower the death benefit. If you need less coverage, ask the insurer to illustrate a smaller amount. Ask about any charge for the change, and about the tax test below.
  • Manage loans. Ask the insurer to illustrate paying loan interest, repaying part of a loan or pausing new loans.
  • In some cases, an exchange to another policy. This is a replacement. It is suitable only some of the time.
Before you replace a policy, including a 1035 exchange: A new policy has its own costs and its own surrender charge period, and the old policy may deduct surrender charges. A claim in a new policy’s first two years can be denied over inaccurate statements, and suicide limits can start again. If your health has changed, new coverage can cost more or be declined. State replacement rules apply. In Virginia, for example, 14VAC5-30 requires the agent to present a replacement notice, Form 30-A, read it to you unless you decline, and leave it with you. You get at least 10 days from delivery to examine the new policy. Paying for a new policy with money from the old one is a replacement too.

A review cannot promise a result. It lays out your options and their costs so you can decide. There is no fee for our help. If a new policy is placed through us, the insurer pays us a commission.

MEC and 1035 basics

General education, not tax advice. Ask a tax professional before you act.

  • Modified endowment contract (MEC). Under 26 U.S.C. 7702A, a policy entered into on or after June 21, 1988 is a MEC if it fails the 7-pay test. It fails when the amount paid in during the first 7 contract years is more than the law’s limit. Under 26 U.S.C. 72, a loan from a MEC is treated as a distribution.
  • Why it matters in a review. In the first 7 contract years, a large catch-up premium can cross that limit. Ask the insurer for your MEC limit before you send one. A cut in benefits in those years is tested as if the policy had been issued at the lower level.
  • 1035 exchange. Under 26 U.S.C. 1035, no gain or loss is recognized when a life insurance contract is exchanged for another life insurance contract. If you also receive money or other property, 26 U.S.C. 1031(b) says gain is recognized up to that amount. Ask how a policy loan is treated. A policy received in exchange for a MEC is a MEC. These are tax rules only. The cautions above still apply.

What to bring

  • Your annual statement.
  • The in-force illustration, if you have it. If not, we can help you word the request.
  • Your original sales illustration.
  • A record of premiums paid, and any loan statements.

You do not need to send health records, a Social Security number or a policy number to start. To ask for a review, use the IUL review form on this page, or first read how indexed universal life works.

Sources

  • NAIC, Life Insurance Illustrations, last updated January 8, 2026.
  • NAIC, Life Insurance Illustrations Model Regulation (Model 582), adopted 1995, text dated April 2001.
  • NAIC, Life Insurance Buyer’s Guide, copyright 2026.
  • Virginia Administrative Code, 14VAC5-30, life insurance and annuity replacements, read November 25, 2026.
  • Virginia Form 30-A, replacement notice, effective April 2007.
  • United States Code, 26 U.S.C. 7702A, 1035, 1031 and 72, current through Public Law 119-142 (November 10, 2026).

faq.a: It is the insurer's updated projection of a life insurance policy you already own. It starts from today's cash value, loans and premium and shows future years in guaranteed and non-guaranteed columns. The NAIC model rule defines it as an illustration furnished after a policy has been in force for one year or more. For index-linked policies sold on or after December 14, 2020, NAIC guideline AG 49-A applies those illustration rules.

faq.q: How do I get an in-force illustration for my IUL?
faq.a: Call or write to the insurer's policy service office as the policy owner. Ask for an in-force illustration at your current premium, with any loan included. The NAIC model notice also lists contacting your agent. Under the NAIC model rule the insurer furnishes one when the owner asks. States decide whether and how to adopt the model, so your state's rule can differ.

Yes. An IUL is a universal life policy, and the NAIC Life Insurance Buyer's Guide says universal life lets you choose a flexible premium pattern as long as you pay enough to keep the policy in force. An in-force illustration shows whether the guaranteed column reaches zero at your current premium, and in what year.

faq.q: How do I know if my IUL is underfunded?
faq.a: Compare the premium you pay with the premium in your original illustration. Then read the guaranteed column of a new in-force illustration. If it reaches zero earlier than you need coverage, ask the insurer what premium would carry the policy to the age you choose.

faq.q: When do IUL surrender charges end?
faq.a: It depends on your policy. Ask the insurer for the surrender charge by policy year. An illustration shows the value available on surrender after surrender charges, loans and loan interest, so you can see the difference year by year.

faq.q: Should I replace my IUL with a 1035 exchange?
faq.a: Only in some cases. A replacement brings new costs and a new surrender charge period. A claim in a new policy's first two years can be denied over inaccurate statements, and suicide limits can start again. A change in health can raise the cost or lead to a decline. State replacement rules, such as Virginia's, require a written notice first. Compare keeping and adjusting your current policy first. Tax points here are general education, not tax advice.

facts.claim: An in-force illustration is an illustration furnished after the policy has been in force for one year or more.
facts.page_date: NAIC Model Laws, Regulations, Guidelines and Other Resources, April 2001 (model adopted 1995)
facts.quote: an illustration furnished at any time after the policy that it depicts has been in force for one year or more

facts.claim: After the first policy anniversary, the policy owner may request updates on the policy's performance; these are in-force illustrations.
facts.quote: After the first policy anniversary, the company may choose to provide, or the policy owner may request, periodic updates on the policy's performance.

facts.claim: The NAIC page calls these updates in-force illustrations.
facts.quote: These updates are provided in the form of in-force illustrations.

facts.claim: Policy charges come out of the policy (cash) value; the model annual report for universal life lists amounts credited and debited by type, such as mortality and expense.
facts.page_date: NAIC Model Laws, Regulations, Guidelines and Other Resources, April 2001 (model adopted 1995)
facts.quote: The total amounts that have been credited or debited to the policy value during the current report period, identifying each by type

facts.claim: The annual statement for a universal life policy shows any outstanding loan, so the loan line can be compared year to year.
facts.page_date: NAIC Model Laws, Regulations, Guidelines and Other Resources, April 2001 (model adopted 1995)
facts.quote: The amount of outstanding loans, if any, as of the end of the current report period

facts.claim: Under the model rule the insurer furnishes an in-force illustration when the policy owner asks.
facts.page_date: NAIC Model Laws, Regulations, Guidelines and Other Resources, April 2001 (model adopted 1995)
facts.quote: Upon the request of the policy owner, the insurer shall furnish an in force illustration of current and future benefits and values

facts.claim: The model notice to owners says an illustration may be requested once a year without charge.
facts.page_date: NAIC Model Laws, Regulations, Guidelines and Other Resources, April 2001 (model adopted 1995)
facts.quote: You may annually request, without charge, such an illustration

facts.claim: The model notice says to contact the state insurance department if the illustration does not arrive within 30 days.
facts.page_date: NAIC Model Laws, Regulations, Guidelines and Other Resources, April 2001 (model adopted 1995)
facts.quote: If you do not receive a current illustration of your policy within 30 days from your request, you should contact your state insurance department.

facts.claim: Model 582 is a model regulation that the NAIC encourages states to adopt; each state decides whether and how to adopt it, so state rules can differ.
facts.quote: The NAIC encourages states to adopt model laws and regulations designed to inform and protect insurance consumers.

facts.claim: Guaranteed elements are the premiums, benefits, values, credits or charges that are guaranteed and set at issue.
facts.page_date: NAIC Model Laws, Regulations, Guidelines and Other Resources, April 2001 (model adopted 1995)
facts.quote: the premiums, benefits, values, credits or charges under a policy of life insurance that are guaranteed and determined at issue

facts.claim: Non-guaranteed elements are those not guaranteed or not set at issue (Virginia's replacement rule uses the same definition).
facts.page_date: Page dated 11/25/2026 (date read); section last amended Virginia Register Volume 23, Issue 9, eff. April 1, 2007
facts.quote: under a life insurance policy or an annuity contract that are not guaranteed or not determined at issue

facts.claim: Guaranteed values are shown before the matching non-guaranteed values.
facts.page_date: NAIC Model Laws, Regulations, Guidelines and Other Resources, April 2001 (model adopted 1995)
facts.quote: The guaranteed elements, if any, shall be shown before corresponding non-guaranteed elements

facts.claim: Where there is no guaranteed value in a year, the guaranteed column shows a zero.
facts.page_date: NAIC Model Laws, Regulations, Guidelines and Other Resources, April 2001 (model adopted 1995)
facts.quote: a zero shall be displayed in the guaranteed column

facts.claim: Illustrated non-guaranteed values must carry a statement that they are not guaranteed, that the insurer can change the assumptions, and that actual results may be more or less favorable.
facts.page_date: NAIC Model Laws, Regulations, Guidelines and Other Resources, April 2001 (model adopted 1995)
facts.quote: The assumptions on which they are based are subject to change by the insurer

facts.claim: Non-guaranteed elements are subject to change. A current cap or participation rate that the policy does not guarantee is a non-guaranteed element under the model rule's definition, so the insurer can change it within the policy's guaranteed limits (owner-required IUL caveat; the source does not name caps or participation rates).
facts.page_date: NAIC Model Laws, Regulations, Guidelines and Other Resources, April 2001 (model adopted 1995)
facts.quote: any non-guaranteed elements illustrated are subject to change and could be either higher or lower

facts.claim: Surrender charges reduce what the owner receives on surrender; an illustration shows the surrender value after surrender charges, policy loans and loan interest.
facts.page_date: NAIC Model Laws, Regulations, Guidelines and Other Resources, April 2001 (model adopted 1995)
facts.quote: the amount available to the policy owner in a lump sum after deduction of surrender charges, policy loans and policy loan interest

facts.claim: Universal life premiums are flexible only as long as enough is paid to keep the policy in force, so an IUL can lapse.
facts.quote: you can choose a flexible premium payment pattern as long as you pay enough to keep your policy in force

facts.claim: For flexible premium universal life, the model annual report must warn when the policy will not stay in force without more premium.
facts.page_date: NAIC Model Laws, Regulations, Guidelines and Other Resources, April 2001 (model adopted 1995)
facts.quote: will not maintain insurance in force until the end of the next reporting period unless further premium payments are made

facts.claim: The insurer can provide statements and illustrations for a policy review.
facts.quote: The insurance company can provide policy statements and illustrations to help with this review.

facts.claim: A replacement has costs, and surrender charges may be deducted from the old policy.
facts.quote: You will pay acquisition costs and there may be surrender costs deducted from your policy or contract.

facts.quote: Acquisition costs for the old policy may have been paid, you will incur costs for the new one.

facts.claim: On a new policy, a claim can be denied for up to the first two years based on inaccurate statements.

facts.quote: Suicide limitations may begin anew on the new coverage.

facts.claim: If health has changed, new coverage can cost more or be declined.
facts.quote: If your health has changed since you bought your old policy, the new one could cost you more, or you could be turned down.

facts.quote: A replacement may not be in your best interest, or your decision could be a good one.

facts.claim: The non-guaranteed column assumes the currently illustrated non-guaranteed elements continue unchanged in every year (wording the model rule requires on a sales illustration).
